title: Chandragupta II Ends the Satraps
subtitle: When Silver Fell Silent: Chandragupta II and the Last of the Saka Satraps
era: End of Western Kshatrapa rule, c. 395-415 CE
moral: When a mint falls silent, an age has ended.

sources.citation: Late coins of Rudrasimha III and western-style coins of Chandragupta II, in E. J. Rapson, British Museum catalogue, 1908
sources.note: Material evidence for the end of Western Kshatrapa coinage and Gupta adoption of western coin forms.

sources.citation: Udayagiri inscription of Virasena, minister of Chandragupta II, c. 401 CE
sources.note: Primary evidence for Gupta presence and western campaigning context.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Pearson, 2008, pp. 450-455
sources.note: Modern synthesis of Chandragupta II's western campaign and its economic significance.

panels.shot: split composition, half showing a fading satrap coin over a coastal port, half a rising Gupta emperor over new silver

dialogue.text: For nearly four hundred years the Saka satraps ruled the western seas, until Chandragupta II took their mints, their ports, and their place—leaving only silent coins to tell how an age ended.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of an ancient silver coin spinning in mid-air

dialogue.text: Long before Chandragupta II, Saka satraps stamped silver at western ports, their coins ringing from Bharuch to distant seas.

panels.shot: wide aerial of the western coast showing ports and inland routes

dialogue.text: These coins carried more than metal. They tied Malwa’s uplands to Gujarat’s harbours and to the wider trade of the Indian Ocean.

panels.shot: mirrored medium shot, both rulers in profile facing opposite directions

dialogue.text: By the late fourth century, Rudrasimha III held the last Kshatrapa throne, as Chandragupta II rose in the east, his gaze turning steadily toward the western sea.

panels.shot: interior court wide shot contrasting two thrones side by side in split-scene

dialogue.text: The Gupta realm was expanding, its revenues swelling. The old satrap domain, rich in ports and silver, now stood as a tempting, vulnerable neighbour.

panels.shot: close-up on Chandragupta II and his minister studying an inscription slab map

dialogue.text: Around 401 CE, his minister Virasena recorded at Udayagiri that the emperor ‘conquered the whole of the western region.’ The inscription is brief, but its shadow is long.

panels.shot: low-angle wide shot of Udayagiri hill with royal entourage

dialogue.text: At Udayagiri near Vidisha, the hill echoed with chisels and chants as Gupta power marked the stone, even as plans for the western march took shape.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chandragupta II in war council over campaign map

dialogue.text: “Malwa, then the coast. Guard the routes, spare the merchants,” Chandragupta II says.

panels.shot: wide shot of two armies facing each other on a dusty plain, but with no combat shown

dialogue.text: The chronicles are silent on the battles. We know only that Gupta power pressed westward, and the satrap forces could not finally hold.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Rudrasimha III in his mint, watching coins being struck

dialogue.text: Rudrasimha III continued to issue silver, his name and title in Saka letters. But his line would be the last to do so.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of two coins side by side, one satrap, one Gupta western-style

dialogue.text: Then the pattern changes. The Kshatrapa coins of Rudrasimha III cease, and new silver appears—Gupta, yet struck in the old western style.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chandragupta II inspecting newly struck western-style coins

dialogue.text: “Let their traders see a known face, and read a new name,” he murmurs.

panels.shot: aerial view of Bharuch harbour now under Gupta banners

dialogue.text: Control of Malwa and Gujarat brought Bharuch’s harbour into Gupta hands, its customs, tolls and sea-routes now feeding a north Indian court far from the surf.

panels.shot: medium shot of merchants exchanging Gupta western-style coins in a market

dialogue.text: Merchants in the western markets now counted Gupta coins, their trust eased by the familiar shape, their allegiance gently redirected by the altered legend.

panels.shot: somber interior shot of a silent, abandoned satrap mint

dialogue.text: Archaeologists and numismatists, centuries later, would notice what contemporaries heard as a faint stop: the western satrap mints fell silent.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern scholar’s hand holding Rudrasimha III’s coin with reflection of Chandragupta II statue in glass

dialogue.text: From Rapson’s catalogues to later histories, the last coins of Rudrasimha III mark the vanishing of the Western Kshatrapas and the rise of Gupta control over the western sea.

panels.shot: medium two-shot of Rudrasimha III fading, Chandragupta II solid, against a backdrop of maps and coins

dialogue.text: No inscription records the last day of Rudrasimha III, but the coinage tells us enough: a dynasty ended, a new order claimed its mints, and trade itself became a prize of empire.

panels.shot: close-up of a hand stopping one die and raising another, symbolically

dialogue.text: When the Gupta emperor took the satrap mints and copied their silver, he did more than conquer land; he captured trust, habit and the flow of wealth along the coast.

panels.shot: wide contemplative shot of waves washing over a buried coin on the shore

dialogue.text: An age can end without a final battle cry; sometimes it ends when a coin is struck for the last time—and another, in a new name, takes its place.
